justifications.functional_suitability: The architecture satisfies R-01 via 'Rules Engine Core', R-02 through 'Case Management System Frontend' and 'Case Service', and R-03 using 'Model Registry Loader' and WebAssembly hot-reloading for zero-downtime updates.
justifications.performance_efficiency: The architecture achieves 3,000 TPS under 50 ms via Go microservices, asynchronous audit emission to 'Amazon SQS / Kinesis', and low-latency 'Hot Feature Table'. However, routing real-time gRPC authorizations through 'Amazon API Gateway' introduces unnecessary proxy latency.
justifications.compatibility: The design interfaces cleanly with 'Payment Processor Systems / Acquirer' over gRPC with mTLS, supports standard HTTPS/TLS 1.3 for analyst web traffic, and integrates standard AWS services.
justifications.usability: The 'Case Management System Frontend' explicitly serves analysts with dedicated components ('Case Queue Component', 'Transaction Details Component', 'Rule Management Component', and 'Audit Log Viewer Component') aligned with their daily operational workflows.
justifications.reliability: 'Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics', DLQs, and FIFO queues provide observability and message durability. However, the system lacks an explicit fallback or fail-open bypass mechanism at the ingress layer to satisfy R-07 when scoring becomes unavailable.
justifications.security: Strict security mechanisms are present: 'Masking & Security Interceptor' strips PANs, 'AWS KMS' handles envelope encryption, mTLS is enforced, and 'Amazon S3 with Object Lock' combined with KMS digital signatures ensures 7-year tamper-evident auditability.
justifications.maintainability: Well-modularized into decoupled services. The 'Rules Engine Core' leverages WebAssembly to isolate rule evaluation, and serverless managed components ('Compliance Reporting Worker', DynamoDB) keep operational burden low for a small three-engineer team.
justifications.portability: The architecture targets AWS eu-west-1 effectively, but relies heavily on proprietary managed services ('Amazon DynamoDB', 'Amazon API Gateway', 'S3 Object Lock', 'AWS KMS'), creating high cloud lock-in and limiting portability to other environments.

PERF-01.justification: Go on ECS with goroutines and DynamoDB single-digit millisecond latency easily supports <50ms P99 at 3,000 rps. API Gateway HTTP APIs may introduce minor latency jitter, but the synchronous path is lean and offloads audit logging asynchronously to SQS/Kinesis.
sensitivity_points: DynamoDB read latency under high read concurrency
API Gateway VPC link networking overhead
tradeoffs: Using DynamoDB over in-memory cache saves cost but risks tail latency spikes

PERF-02.justification: Workloads are isolated: scoring runs on Go/ECS with separate DynamoDB tables (Hot Feature Table vs Case Management Table), while analysts query Case Management System API on Node.js. Resource contention between analyst operations and real-time scoring is effectively eliminated.
sensitivity_points: Table partitioning and provisioned throughput separation in DynamoDB
tradeoffs: Maintaining separate API services increases operational footprint for a 3-engineer team

AVAIL-01.justification: The architecture lacks an explicit fallback mechanism or circuit breaker at API Gateway or the client boundary to fail open/closed when the scoring engine crashes, creating a risk that payments remain blocked longer than 1 minute.
sensitivity_points: Absence of edge-level fallback routing during scoring engine downtime
tradeoffs: Failing open avoids payment blockage but exposes the acquirer to fraud risk

AVAIL-02.justification: Audit logging is fully decoupled from the real-time scoring path. The engine dispatches audit events asynchronously via the Audit Logger Component to SQS/Kinesis with DLQs, guaranteeing that slow or failing downstream audit stores do not degrade latency or lose records.
sensitivity_points: Queue buffer retention limits during extended audit store outages
tradeoffs: Asynchronous buffering guarantees latency but introduces eventual consistency for audit log persistence

MOD-01.justification: Rules Engine Core supports Wasm sandboxing and hot-reloading via Model Registry Loader polling S3, alongside a Shadow Evaluator for testing. Fast rollback is supported by pointing back to previous Wasm models without redeploying containers.
sensitivity_points: Model polling frequency and dynamic memory overhead in Wasm runtime
tradeoffs: Wasm execution provides sandboxed hot updates but may incur slight CPU overhead versus native Go

MOD-02.justification: Analysts can update rules via the Rule Management Component in the frontend through Case Management API. Wasm hot-reloading enables zero-downtime activation well within 1 hour, and decision payloads store rule evaluation outputs for auditability.
sensitivity_points: Rule validation pipeline prior to distribution to prevent runtime panic
tradeoffs: Hot-reloading rules at runtime without restarts increases the risk of undetected logical regressions

SEC-01.justification: The Case Management System API features a dedicated Masking & Security Interceptor stripping PANs and validating RBAC. CloudWatch Alarms, Metric Filters, and KMS protect data; however, explicit automated anomaly detection mechanisms within 15 minutes are only minimally detailed.
sensitivity_points: Completeness of PAN masking logic across all analyst API endpoints
tradeoffs: Strict masking protects cardholder data but limits manual context during deep fraud investigations

SEC-02.justification: Decisions, inputs, and models are signed using AWS KMS ECC_NIST_P256 by the Compliance Reporting Worker and stored in Amazon S3 with Object Lock configured for 7-year tamper-evident retention. Querying daily Parquet digests guarantees retrieval within one working day.
sensitivity_points: Immutability policies on S3 Object Lock and KMS key rotation lifecycle
tradeoffs: Parquet cold storage on S3 reduces 7-year storage costs but requires batch scanning to reproduce single decisions
